data.reason: The KPI's main goal is town-wide on_time_deliveries, with p95_wait_s, max_wait_s and unfinished as watched goals (K1). Option 1 lowers on-time from 219.4 to 216.4 (-3.0, 0/5 seeds improved), so it fails the objective gate on every seed. It also worsens every customer-facing metric. Late rises from 3.4 to 6.4, p95_wait_s from 93.2 to 108 and max_wait_s from 224 to 234. Road violations rise from 34.8 to 58.0 and blocked s from 1217 to 1492. I follow the LLM's recommendation. I am choosing against the B and C majority vote for option 1. Customers have no vote, and the harm to them is consistent across seeds. In D1 I overrode B and C because there was a clear customer gain (+9.2, 5/5). Here the evidence points the other way: B and C gain at a measured cost to customers. I acknowledge the D1 commitment to C. C remains far behind at 46.9, and this decision delays the mitigation again. That is a real cost to C's trust, and I take responsibility for it on behalf of the operator. But the KPI the operator set does not name company fairness. Removing the sanction entirely would loosen road-rule enforcement and push violations up sharply, while the cause of the D1 violation rise is still unexamined. The promise to C should be met by a mitigation that does not cost customers. Candidates are an intermediate sanction_lambda, a negotiated compensation, or a rule change that targets C's bottleneck. These must be measured on the same seeds before the next period. No contract change is involved, so customers' promised times are unaffected.
assumptions: The 5-seed measurement represents next period's busy demand well enough that the -3.0 on-time loss under option 1 is real.
Keeping v2 leaves the metrics near the current values (on-time 219.4, late 3.4, p95_wait_s 93.2).
C will keep participating in the next period despite the delayed mitigation.
Other mitigation routes for C (intermediate sanction values, compensation) are feasible within the rules and the constitution.
unknowns: Whether intermediate sanction_lambda values (e.g. 0.25) would raise C's utility at little or no customer cost.
Why C's utility depends so strongly on the sanction, and whether C's robots overstay by policy.
How C will respond to a second delay of the D1 mitigation (voting behaviour, cooperation, exit).
Whether the road violations at the current 34.8 level, or the 58.0 level under option 1, are safety-relevant.
Next period's demand and how it changes the trade-off.
Per-seed wait data for option 1 and for the current rules.
